description: Apple scab is one of the most common and destructive fungal diseases of apple trees, caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis. It thrives in cool, moist spring conditions and can defoliate trees and render fruit unmarketable. Repeated annual infections can weaken the tree and significantly reduce yield quality and quantity.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety or corky lesions on the upper surface of leaves
Lesions on fruit that become dark, sunken, and cracked as they enlarge
Yellowing and premature drop of heavily infected leaves
Distorted, misshapen fruit in cases of early-season infection
Dark, circular scabby spots on twigs and shoots
causes: Fungal pathogen Venturia inaequalis overwinters in infected fallen leaves and shoots
Spores are released during wet, cool spring weather (10–24°C) and spread by rain splash and wind
Prolonged leaf wetness periods (6+ hours) favour spore germination and infection
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties such as 'Liberty', 'Enterprise', or 'GoldRush'
Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to reduce overwintering inoculum
Prune trees to improve air circulation and reduce canopy humidity
Apply preventive fungicide sprays starting at green-tip stage and through the primary scab season
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation to minimise leaf wetness
management: Apply registered fungicides (e.g., captan, myclobutanil, or mancozeb) on a 7–10 day schedule during wet periods
Use infection period models (e.g., Mills table) to time sprays accurately
Remove and destroy heavily infected fruit and leaves to reduce secondary inoculum
Consult local agricultural experts for specific pesticide recommendations and dosages.

description: Black rot of apple is caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa and affects the fruit, leaves, and bark of apple trees. The disease is particularly damaging in warm, wet summers and can cause extensive fruit rot and limb cankers that girdle and kill branches. All above-ground parts of the tree are susceptible.
symptoms: Circular, brown rotted areas on fruit beginning at the calyx end that turn black and mummified
Purple-bordered leaf spots ('frog-eye' lesions) with a tan center and purple halo
Reddish-brown, sunken cankers on branches and trunks that may girdle and kill limbs
Pycnidia (small black fungal fruiting bodies) visible on mummified fruit and bark cankers
Fruit may shrivel and become hard, black 'mummies' that remain on the tree
causes: Fungal pathogen Botryosphaeria obtusa overwinters in mummified fruit, bark cankers, and dead wood
Spores spread by rain splash and wind during warm (21–30°C), wet conditions
Wounds from pruning, hail, or insects provide entry points for the fungus
prevention: Remove and destroy mummified fruit from the tree and ground during winter pruning
Prune out dead or cankered wood and disinfect pruning tools between cuts
Maintain overall tree health through proper fertilization and irrigation
Apply preventive fungicide sprays from pink stage through harvest
Control fire blight infections and insect borers that create wounds for black rot entry
management: Apply registered fungicides such as captan or thiophanate-methyl during the growing season
Remove all infected material and cankers promptly to limit spread
Improve air circulation through strategic pruning to reduce humidity within the canopy
Consult local agricultural experts for specific pesticide recommendations and dosages.
disclaimer: Consult local agricultural experts for specific pesticide recommendations and dosages.

description: Cedar apple rust is caused by Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae, a fungus that requires two host plants — eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) and apple — to complete its life cycle. Bright orange, gelatinous spore horns appear on cedar galls in spring and release spores that infect apple leaves and fruit. Though rarely fatal, repeated infections weaken trees and reduce fruit quality.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper surface of apple leaves in spring
Spots enlarge and develop orange, tube-like structures (aecia) on the undersides of leaves
Similar lesions can appear on young fruit, causing deformation and premature drop
Severely infected leaves may yellow and drop early
On cedar hosts, rusty-brown galls with orange gelatinous tendrils appear after rain
causes: Fungal pathogen Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae alternates between apple and eastern red cedar hosts
Teliospores from cedar galls are wind-dispersed to apple during moist, cool spring weather
Proximity of apple orchards to cedar or juniper trees greatly increases disease risk
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties such as 'Redfree', 'Williams Pride', or 'Prima'
Remove eastern red cedar and juniper trees within a 1-km radius if feasible
Apply preventive fungicide sprays from the pink bud stage through the first 3–4 weeks after petal fall
Scout cedar trees in late winter and remove rust galls before they produce spores
Maintain good tree nutrition to support overall resistance
management: Apply registered fungicides (e.g., myclobutanil, trifloxystrobin) on a 7–10 day schedule during the infection period
Time sprays to coincide with wet periods when cedar galls are producing spores
Remove infected leaves and fruit to reduce secondary spread where practical
Consult local agricultural experts for specific pesticide recommendations and dosages.

prevention: Plant powdery mildew-resistant or tolerant cherry varieties where available
Prune to open up the canopy and improve air movement through the tree
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization, which produces succulent shoots susceptible to infection
Begin protective fungicide applications at the first sign of budbreak in high-risk orchards
Remove and destroy mummified fruit and diseased shoot tips during dormant pruning
management: Apply registered fungicides such as sulphur, myclobutanil, or trifloxystrobin at 7–14 day intervals
Alternate between fungicide classes to prevent the development of resistance
Remove and destroy heavily infected shoots and leaves to reduce inoculum load

disease: Cercospora Leaf Spot / Gray Leaf Spot
description: Gray leaf spot, caused by the fungal pathogen Cercospora zeae-maydis, is one of the most economically important foliar diseases of maize worldwide. The disease thrives under warm, humid conditions with extended periods of leaf wetness and can cause significant yield losses by killing leaf tissue before grain fill is complete. It is especially problematic in conservation tillage systems where infected crop residue persists.
symptoms: Small, tan spots with yellow halos that elongate into narrow, rectangular grey-brown lesions running parallel to leaf veins
Lesions eventually coalesce, turning entire leaves grey and causing them to die
Disease progresses from lower leaves upward in the canopy
In severe cases, whole plants may appear scorched or dead by silking and grain fill stages
Dusty grey fungal sporulation visible on lesion surfaces under humid conditions
causes: Fungal pathogen Cercospora zeae-maydis survives on infected maize residue left on the soil surface
Warm temperatures (25–30°C) combined with high humidity and prolonged leaf wetness (12+ hours) promote infection
Minimum tillage and continuous maize cultivation increase inoculum pressure
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant maize hybrids, the single most effective management strategy
Rotate crops to break the disease cycle and reduce residue-borne inoculum
Till crop residues to accelerate decomposition and reduce surface inoculum
Avoid late planting that extends grain fill into periods of high humidity
Ensure balanced fertility, particularly adequate potassium, to support plant health
management: Apply foliar fungicides (e.g., strobilurins, triazoles, or premixes) at VT/R1 growth stage when disease appears on the third leaf below the ear
Scout fields regularly from V6 onwards in high-risk areas to time sprays accurately
Consider economic thresholds before applying fungicides in lower-risk environments
Consult local agricultural experts for specific pesticide recommendations and dosages.
disclaimer: Consult local agricultural experts for specific pesticide recommendations and dosages.

description: Common rust of maize is caused by Puccinia sorghi and is a widespread foliar disease that occurs in most maize-growing areas of the world. The pathogen is an obligate parasite that spreads primarily by wind-blown urediniospores blown in from tropical overwintering regions each season. While commonly seen, it typically causes economic losses only in susceptible hybrids when infections occur early in the season.
symptoms: Small, circular to elongate, brick-red to brown pustules (uredinia) scattered across both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture through the leaf epidermis and release powdery, rust-coloured spores
Heavily infected leaves may turn yellow then brown as pustules coalesce
Late-season black telia (overwintering spore structures) may replace uredinia
Disease pressure is greatest in cool to moderate temperatures (16–23°C) with high humidity
causes: Fungal pathogen Puccinia sorghi is an obligate parasite that overwinters in tropical/subtropical regions and spreads northward on wind currents each season
Cool, moist weather with extended dew periods promotes spore germination and infection
Susceptible hybrids and early planting may increase vulnerability
prevention: Plant rust-resistant or tolerant maize hybrids; resistance is widely available
Early planting can allow the crop to mature before high rust pressure builds
Monitor fields regularly, especially in cool, moist years
Avoid over-application of nitrogen, which can increase tissue susceptibility
Rotate crops to break cycles of other soilborne pathogens that stress plants
management: Apply registered foliar fungicides (e.g., triazoles, strobilurins) if disease appears before tasselling in susceptible hybrids
Economic spraying is usually warranted only when disease is present on the ear leaf or above before silking
Scout fields to determine actual disease levels before making spray decisions
Consult local agricultural experts for specific pesticide recommendations and dosages.
disclaimer: Consult local agricultural experts for specific pesticide recommendations and dosages.

description: Northern leaf blight (NLB) is caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum (formerly Helminthosporium turcicum) and is a major foliar disease of maize in temperate production regions worldwide. Large lesions can rapidly coalesce and kill significant proportions of leaf area, dramatically reducing photosynthetic capacity and grain fill. The disease is most severe when infections occur before tasselling.
symptoms: Long (5–15 cm), elliptical or cigar-shaped, grey-green to tan lesions on leaves
Lesions run parallel to leaf veins and may appear water-soaked initially
Dark green to grey sporulation visible in the centre of lesions under humid conditions
Multiple lesions can coalesce, causing large areas of leaf death
Disease begins on lower leaves and progresses upward; severe early infection causes general blighting of the plant
causes: Fungal pathogen Exserohilum turcicum overwinters on infected maize residue on or in the soil
Moderate temperatures (18–25°C) and prolonged leaf wetness (6–18 hours) favour infection and spore production
Conservation tillage systems that leave residue on the surface increase inoculum levels
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids; multiple resistance genes (Ht1, Ht2, HtN, htm1) are available
Rotate maize with non-host crops such as soybean or wheat to reduce inoculum
Till crop residues to speed decomposition
Plant at optimal density to avoid excessive canopy humidity
Scout from V6 onwards in areas with a history of NLB
management: Apply registered foliar fungicides (e.g., azoxystrobin, propiconazole) at VT/R1 if disease is detected on or above the ear leaf before tasselling in susceptible hybrids
Time fungicide applications to target early infection periods for best economic return
Consider economic thresholds and hybrid susceptibility before applying fungicides

description: Grape black rot, caused by the fungus Guignardia bidwellii, is one of the most destructive diseases of grapes in humid climates. It attacks all green tissue including leaves, shoots, and berries, and can cause total crop loss in unmanaged vineyards. Mummified berries that remain on the vine serve as the primary source of inoculum for subsequent seasons.
symptoms: Small, circular, light brown spots with a dark border on leaves, surrounded by a yellow halo

Infected berries turn brown, then shrivel and become hard, black mummies that remain on the cluster
Shoot lesions appear as dark, slightly sunken cankers
Stem and tendril infections cause dark brown streaking
causes: Fungal pathogen Guignardia bidwellii overwinters in mummified berries and infected canes left on or hanging from the vine
Ascospores and conidia are released during warm, wet weather and spread by rain splash and wind
Warm temperatures (20–30°C) with 6+ hours of leaf wetness are optimal for infection
prevention: Remove and destroy all mummified berries and infected canes during dormant pruning
Train vines to open canopy systems (e.g., VSP, Geneva Double Curtain) to maximise airflow
Apply preventive fungicide sprays from budbreak through veraison
Scout vineyards frequently during shoot growth and flowering periods
Avoid planting in low-lying areas with poor air drainage
management: Apply registered fungicides such as mancozeb, myclobutanil, or azoxystrobin on a 7–10 day spray program during critical periods
Remove infected material from the vineyard to reduce inoculum
Increase spray frequency during prolonged wet periods

description: Esca, also known as black measles, is a destructive trunk disease complex of grapevines caused by several wood-colonising fungi including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium minimum, and Fomitiporia mediterranea. These fungi invade through pruning wounds and progressively destroy internal wood tissue, eventually causing vine decline and death. It is widespread in vineyards worldwide and has no curative chemical treatment once wood is infected.
symptoms: Interveinal leaf chlorosis (yellowing) and necrosis, giving leaves a 'tiger-stripe' pattern
Berry skin develops small, dark-brown to black spots or speckling ('measles') near harvest

Sudden 'apoplexy' — rapid wilting and death of entire canes or vines — can occur in hot weather
causes: Multiple fungal pathogens (Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium minimum, Fomitiporia mediterranea) colonise wood via pruning wounds
Spores are spread by wind, rain, and pruning tools; infection primarily occurs through fresh pruning wounds
Stress factors such as drought, waterlogging, and other diseases exacerbate vine decline
prevention: Prune in dry weather and avoid making cuts during or just before rainy periods to reduce infection risk
Apply wound sealants or biological protectants to pruning cuts immediately after pruning
Disinfect pruning tools between vines with 70% ethanol or 2% sodium hypochlorite solutions
Remove and destroy infected wood and severely affected vines promptly
Establish new vineyards with certified, pathogen-free planting material
management: No curative fungicides are available for established wood infections; management focuses on slowing progression
Remedial surgery — removing and retraining new canes from healthy wood — may prolong vine life
Manage vine water stress through appropriate irrigation to reduce apoplexy risk

description: Huanglongbing (HLB), commonly known as citrus greening, is considered the most devastating citrus disease in the world, caused by the bacteria Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (CLas) and transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri). Infected trees produce small, misshapen, bitter fruit and gradually decline over several years until they die. There is currently no cure; management focuses on controlling the psyllid vector and removing infected trees.
symptoms: Blotchy mottling of leaves — asymmetric, irregular yellow blotching that does not follow vein patterns (distinguishes it from nutrient deficiency)

causes: Phloem-limited bacteria Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (Asia) or CLam (Americas) are transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid Diaphorina citri during feeding
Infected budwood used for propagation can spread the disease to new plantings
No cure exists; infected trees act as a continuous reservoir of inoculum for psyllid-mediated spread
prevention: Use certified, disease-free nursery budwood and planting material
Implement rigorous Asian citrus psyllid (ACP) monitoring and management using systemic insecticides
Establish insect-proof nursery structures for propagation
Quarantine zones and movement restrictions on citrus plant material help slow regional spread
Remove and destroy HLB-positive trees promptly to reduce inoculum source for psyllids
management: No curative treatment is available; infected trees should be removed and destroyed to protect surrounding trees
Control psyllid populations with systemic insecticides (neonicotinoids, organophosphates) on a programmatic basis to reduce transmission

description: Early blight of potato is caused by the fungal pathogen Alternaria solani and is a common, widespread disease that reduces yield by causing premature defoliation.
